hook: Most people treat self-critical thoughts as truth because they're delivered in first person. Your inner critic sounds like you. It isn't you.
topic: The grammar of self-criticism — and how to create observer distance
body:
**"I'm not good enough." "I always ruin things." "Nobody really respects me."**

These feel like observations because they come in the first person. They have the grammar of self-knowledge.

But the inner critic didn't originate with you. It was constructed from the outside in — from environments, relationships, and early experiences where criticism was the language being spoken. You absorbed the voice, internalised its tone, and now it runs automatically in your register.

The fact that it sounds like you is not evidence that it is you.

Here's a simple practice: when the critic speaks, name it in the third person. Not "I'm not good enough." Instead: "The critic is telling me I'm not good enough." That one shift — from I to the critic — creates grammatical distance. And distance is not the same as denial. You're not pretending the thought isn't there. You're just refusing to let it speak as though it has final authority.

Over time, that practice changes not just how you respond to the thought — but how much power the thought has when it arrives.

Free guide is in my bio.
